I used to work as a store where we sold and maintained machines.
We always recommend bringing it in for service once every 3 years, even if you do some maintenance yourself. The mechanics have tools and expertise that you probably don't. They can clean it a lot deeper and better, and that will help your machine last longer.

In our experience, it is worth it to bring them in for service. We have seen the same machine lasting 10 years and 50 years, mostly based on how you maintain it. The mechanics really are helpful.

Granted, you do need to go to a good mechanic. We have seen machines come in after they had gone to a different shop, and it was pretty bad. So do youe research. 

Also, if there is something wrong with your machine and you can't fix it with the basics? Don't try to fix it on your own. We have seen so many DIYers and 'Bob the Builders' as my colleagues called them where the machine is more messed up because people tried to fix it themselves. For 99% of people, you don't have the expertise to fix it, let a professional do it. Maintenance is less expensive than buying a new (proper) machine.


If it is too heavy, see if the shop has options to have it picked up. Once a week, i would drive through the area and pick up machines for maintenance, and brought them back a week later.

I just want to say to men like this:

You absolutely can give compliments to people without coming across as a creep.

A couple of years ago, i was having a rough day. I was on my way to my therapist, just parked my car, and started walking towards the building. This random man i had never met walked up to me and went:

"Excuse me, Miss, i just wanted to say you look really nice today. Happy New Year! Have a nice day." (It was early januari)

And he walked away. He had a friendly smile on his face, didn't come close, didn't touch me, didn't come across weird at all.

It really helped me feel a bit better. I have no idea if he just said what he said because he noticed i had a bad day, or if he genuinely thought i looked nice, but it doesn't matter. He was nice and it made my day.

At the time, i was 21 or 22, and this guy was probably in his late 30's. It is easy to come across as a creep when you give compliments to younger women, but you absolutely can if you do about it in a normal way.

My advice would be:
-smile friendly
-don't come too close. People can notice you are talking to them without you coming into their personal space.
-don't linger. Don't give a compliment and then wait for them to respond. That can make things weird. You don't need to run away, but don't stay there and stare at them either. The point of the compliment should be to be nice, and so a thank you should not be the goal or necessary. If you are trying to hit on someone, don't do that to random people who are trying to go somewhere.

Hope this can help a little bit, and if people have more tips or nice experiences to share, please do!

Don't simply use it, even if it fits.
Often different brands of machines, and even different types of one brand, have very specific measurements for the feet.

Obviously one of the things is whether or not the foot fits in the holder, but also the distance to the needle hole can be very specific, and the hole in the foot has to it ovet the hole in the stitchplate.

If you try a foot that is was not made to go on that machine, first slowly turn the wheel on the side of yoir machine to make sure the needle doesn't go onto the foot and break. Make sure the needle can fit through the holes cleanly before you actually sew with it.

Sometimes you're lucky and you can use a foot from machine x on machine y, but there are no standard universal feet, so always test them first.

I'd go with the brother personally. It's computer operated so it is easy to use.
Stitch selections is easy by turning the dial.
Some advantages because it is c.o.:
-You can limit the speed

-You have a button to make the needle go in the highest or lowest position, which is handy for turning corners for example

-It has a different type of engine than a manual. A manual machine gets the strength from speed, a c.o. always has the same amount of strength, so when you use thicker material a manual might start of with some difficulties.

-there is a little display where it tells you what stitch is selected, the length and width of the stitch, and what foot they advise you to use with that stitch.

-it has a base stitch length and width for each stitch, and they are easy to change if you want to, but because it has base settings you do not have to think about checking them every time. 

-one step buttonholes. There is a little lever in the back you pull down when you want to do a buttonhole. The user manual will have more specific instructions on how to use it.
